records.source: Ὡς οὖν ἔγνω ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἤκουσαν οἱ Φαρισαῖοι ὅτι Ἰησοῦς πλείονας μαθητὰς ποιεῖ καὶ βαπτίζει ἢ Ἰωάννης καίτοιγε Ἰησοῦς αὐτὸς οὐκ ἐβάπτιζεν ἀλλ’ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ἀφῆκεν τὴν Ἰουδαίαν καὶ ἀπῆλθεν πάλιν εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν.
records.gloss: When therefore knew the Jesus that heard the Pharisees that Jesus more disciples makes and baptizes than John \v 2 (although indeed Jesus himself not was baptizing, but the disciples of him), \v 3 he left the Judea and went away again into the Galilee.

L.1: So when Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John
L.2: (although Jesus {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} was not baptizing, but {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples [were]),
L.3: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} left Judea and went away again into Galilee.

R.1: The Pharisees heard that more people were becoming Jesus's disciples than John's, and that Jesus was baptizing them. Jesus knew that they had heard this.
R.2: (Really it was Jesus's disciples who did the baptizing, not Jesus {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.)
R.3: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} left Judea and went back to Galilee.

decisions.choice: Jesus (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, among them some of the oldest, read "the Lord" at the start of the verse; others, including Codex Sinaiticus, read "Jesus", and the SBLGNT follows them. Both name the same person. Before the resurrection John's narrative seldom calls Jesus "the Lord" (6:23; 11:2), and the name comes twice more in these verses, which may have led copyists to vary it one way or the other. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Jesus came to know what the Pharisees had heard; the second "Jesus" belongs to the report they heard
alternatives: Jesus knew it by his own insight (compare 2:25)
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to know or to come to know. The sentence stacks two "that" clauses: Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making more disciples than John. Repeating the name in the second clause shows it is what the Pharisees were told. John has already told how people were going to Jesus rather than to John (3:26).

decisions.choice: an aside correcting the report: Jesus's disciples did the baptizing, not Jesus himself
alternatives: Jesus baptized at first and later stopped
decisions.reason: In 3:22 and 3:26 Jesus is said to baptize. The narrator now adds that the baptizing was done by his disciples, under his authority, so the report is true in substance but not in the letter. The aside also keeps Jesus out of a contest of numbers with John (3:26-30): Jesus is the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit (1:33). The words are in the manuscripts generally.

decisions.choice: the Pharisees: a movement of teachers devoted to keeping the law strictly
decisions.reason: Pharisees were among those who questioned John the Baptist (1:24). Their interest in the growing movement around Jesus is the reason given for his leaving: the sentence makes the departure follow from what they had heard. John does not say what Jesus wished to avoid; later the authorities look for a way to kill him, but his hour has not yet come (5:18; 7:1, 30).

decisions.choice: learned (B); knew that they had heard this (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "learned" because the verb here means coming to know (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps "knew", which can carry the same sense.

decisions.choice: the long sentence split, with verse 2 in parentheses
decisions.reason: The Greek is one sentence with an aside in the middle. Balanced and Readable break it into three and mark the aside with parentheses so that the main line, he left Judea, stays clear.

decisions.choice: more people were becoming Jesus's disciples than John's
decisions.reason: "Making disciples" means gaining followers who learn from a teacher; Readable says it plainly and keeps the word "disciples", as everywhere in John.

records.heading: Jesus and the Samaritan woman

records.source: ἔδει δὲ αὐτὸν διέρχεσθαι διὰ τῆς Σαμαρείας.
records.gloss: It was necessary now [for] him to pass through the Samaria.

L.4: Now it was necessary for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to pass through Samaria.

R.4: Jesus had to go through Samaria.

decisions.choice: had to: a necessity John leaves open; the route required it, and in John "must" also marks what God has planned
alternatives: only the road: the shortest way ran through Samaria
only God's plan: he was sent to this town
decisions.reason: Travelers going north from Judea could go straight through Samaria or go around it by the Jordan valley. Josephus says the road through Samaria took three days and was the one Galileans used on their way to the festivals (Life 269; Antiquities 20.118), so the road alone could explain it. But John uses this verb, ἔδει, for what God's purpose requires: the Son of Man must be lifted up (3:14), he must increase (3:30), he must bring other sheep (10:16). What happens at the well suggests the second sense is present too. The evidence is balanced, so every level says only "had to" and makes neither sense explicit.

decisions.choice: Samaria: the region between Judea and Galilee, home of the Samaritans
decisions.reason: Samaria was first the capital, then the name, of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:24). In Jesus's day it was the land of the Samaritans, who worshiped the God of Israel but were divided from the Jews (verse 9).

decisions.choice: it was necessary (L); had to (B, R)
decisions.reason: Plain words that keep both senses of the necessity open (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus at the start of the journey.

records.source: ἔρχεται οὖν εἰς πόλιν τῆς Σαμαρείας λεγομένην Συχὰρ πλησίον τοῦ χωρίου ὃ ἔδωκεν Ἰακὼβ τῷ Ἰωσὴφ τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ·
records.gloss: He comes therefore to a city of the Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground that gave Jacob to the Joseph the son of him;

L.5: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob gave to Joseph his son.

R.5: He came to a town in Samaria called Sychar. It was near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph long ago.

decisions.choice: Sychar: a town near Shechem whose exact site is not certain
decisions.reason: Only John mentions Sychar. It is usually placed at the village of Askar, a short walk north of the well shown today as Jacob's well, at the foot of Mount Gerizim; others take it to be ancient Shechem, whose ruins lie close to the well. Either way it was near enough for the woman to come from it for water (verses 7, 28).

decisions.choice: the land Jacob gave to Joseph at Shechem
decisions.reason: Jacob bought a plot of ground at Shechem (Genesis 33:18-19), and on his deathbed gave Joseph one portion more than his brothers (Genesis 48:22, where the Hebrew word for "portion" is the same as the name Shechem). Joseph's bones were buried there (Joshua 24:32). The Samaritans, who claimed descent from Joseph, lived in the middle of this history (verse 12).

decisions.choice: town: a settlement with its own community, large or small
decisions.reason: The word is used of any town or village with its own people and life; Sychar was small.

decisions.choice: town
decisions.reason: "City" suggests a large place; this was a country town.

decisions.choice: came
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he comes", "she says") for vividness. Here and through the rest of the passage Balanced and Readable use the past, normal for a story told in this language; Literal keeps the present.

decisions.choice: long ago
decisions.reason: Readable shows that Jacob lived many centuries before.

records.source: ἦν δὲ ἐκεῖ πηγὴ τοῦ Ἰακώβ.
records.gloss: Was now there [the] spring of the Jacob.

L.6: Now the spring of Jacob was there.

decisions.choice: spring: a source of water; here a deep well that reaches spring water
alternatives: a spring flowing at the surface
decisions.reason: The narrator calls it πηγὴ, a spring or source; the woman calls it φρέαρ, a well dug down into the ground (verses 11-12). Both fit a deep well fed by groundwater. The narrator's word prepares for verse 14, where Jesus promises a spring of water within a person.

decisions.choice: Jacob's well: a well tied to Jacob by tradition
decisions.reason: The Old Testament does not tell of Jacob digging a well; the name comes from tradition linked with the land he owned here (verse 5). The woman speaks of Jacob as the one who gave the well (verse 12). A deep well at the foot of Mount Gerizim, near modern Nablus, has been shown as Jacob's well since early Christian times.

decisions.choice: well
decisions.reason: In ordinary speech this is a well, the word the woman uses. Literal keeps "spring" so the link with verse 14 can be seen; there every level says "spring".

records.source: ὁ οὖν Ἰησοῦς κεκοπιακὼς ἐκ τῆς ὁδοιπορίας ἐκαθέζετο οὕτως ἐπὶ τῇ πηγῇ· ὥρα ἦν ὡς ἕκτη.
records.gloss: The therefore Jesus, having become weary from the journey, was sitting thus at the spring; [the] hour was about [the] sixth.

L.6: So Jesus, worn out from the journey, was sitting thus at the spring; [the] hour was about [the] sixth.

R.6: Jesus was tired from the long walk, so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sat down by the well. It was about noon.

decisions.choice: worn out from the journey: Jesus is truly tired
decisions.reason: The verb is used of being tired out by hard work or travel. The Word who became flesh (1:14) is weary here and thirsty (verse 7), as he weeps at 11:35 and thirsts on the cross (19:28).

decisions.choice: thus: just as he was, tired, without more ado
alternatives: on the ground by the well
decisions.reason: The adverb points back to his tiredness: worn out as he was, he simply sat down there. It adds no further fact.

decisions.choice: the sixth hour: about noon
alternatives: about six in the morning or evening, counting the hours from midnight
decisions.reason: Hours were counted from sunrise, about six in the morning (see the note at 1:39), so the sixth hour was midday, the heat of the day. Counting from midnight, which some have proposed for John, would give six in the morning or evening. Genesis 24:11 speaks of evening as the time women went out to draw water; John does not say why this woman came at noon. The same hour is named at 19:14, when Pilate brings Jesus out to the crowd.

decisions.choice: was sitting: the scene is set when the woman arrives
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense describes him seated at the well as the next event happens.

decisions.choice: about noon
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: clock times stay literal at Literal, and Balanced and Readable give the modern time (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: worn out from the journey (L, B); tired from the long walk (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday words for being tired out by travel.

decisions.choice: just as he was
decisions.reason: Gives the sense of the adverb (meaning decision m2); Readable leaves it in "so".

records.source: Ἔρχεται γυνὴ ἐκ τῆς Σαμαρείας ἀντλῆσαι ὕδωρ.
records.gloss: Comes a woman out of the Samaria to draw water.

L.7: A woman from Samaria comes to draw water.

R.7: A woman from Samaria came to get water from the well.

decisions.choice: from Samaria: a woman of the region and its people, a Samaritan
decisions.reason: The old city of Samaria, rebuilt by Herod as Sebaste, lay too far off for her to come here for water. The phrase names her people; verse 9 calls her "the Samaritan woman", and she comes from the nearby town (verse 28).

decisions.choice: a meeting at a well, which in Scripture often leads to a betrothal
decisions.reason: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah at a well (Genesis 24:10-27); Jacob meets Rachel at a well (Genesis 29:1-12); Moses meets Zipporah at a well (Exodus 2:15-21). Here, at Jacob's well, a stranger asks a woman for water, and the talk turns to her husbands (verses 16-18); John the Baptist has just called Jesus the bridegroom (3:29). John does not draw the link himself, so every level tells the meeting plainly.

decisions.choice: A Samaritan woman
decisions.reason: Says what the phrase means (meaning decision m1), as verse 9 does.

decisions.choice: get water from the well
decisions.reason: "Draw" in this sense is not a common word for young readers.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Δός μοι πεῖν·
records.gloss: Says to her the Jesus, "Give me to drink."

L.7: Jesus says to her, "Give {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} [something] to drink."

R.7: Jesus said to her, "Will you give {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} a drink?"

decisions.choice: a request that crosses two lines of custom
decisions.reason: A Jewish man asks a Samaritan woman he does not know for water, and would drink from her vessel. The woman is surprised (verse 9), and so are the disciples later (verse 27). Jesus begins with his own need.

decisions.choice: a request in the form of a command
decisions.reason: The command form was the ordinary way to ask for something; it is not rude.

decisions.choice: Will you give me a drink?
decisions.reason: A bare command can sound rude to young readers; the question keeps it a request (meaning decision m2).

records.source: οἱ γὰρ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ἀπεληλύθεισαν εἰς τὴν πόλιν, ἵνα τροφὰς ἀγοράσωσιν.
records.gloss: The for disciples of him had gone away into the city, so that food they might buy.

L.8: For {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples had gone away into the town to buy food.

R.8: Jesus's disciples had gone into the town to buy food, so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was alone.

decisions.choice: for: explains why Jesus asks her; he was alone
decisions.reason: With the disciples away there was no one else to draw water for him, and verse 11 shows he had nothing to draw with. It also explains why Jesus and the woman talk alone until they return (verse 27).

decisions.choice: buying food in a Samaritan town
decisions.reason: The disciples go to buy food from Samaritans, so the separation described in verse 9 did not rule out every kind of dealing between the two peoples. This bears on what verse 9 means.

decisions.choice: so he was alone
decisions.reason: Readable states what the explanation implies (meaning decision m1).

records.source: λέγει οὖν αὐτῷ ἡ γυνὴ ἡ Σαμαρῖτις· Πῶς σὺ Ἰουδαῖος ὢν παρ’ ἐμοῦ πεῖν αἰτεῖς γυναικὸς Σαμαρίτιδος οὔσης;
records.gloss: Says therefore to him the woman the Samaritan, "How you, a Jew being, from me to drink ask, a woman Samaritan being?"

L.9: So the Samaritan woman says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "How do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, being a Jew, ask to drink from me, being a Samaritan woman?"

R.9: The woman said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You are a Jew, and I am a woman from Samaria. Why are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} asking me for a drink?"

decisions.choice: a Jew: a member of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: She recognizes him as one of the Jewish people, perhaps by his speech or dress. Jesus is a Jew, and in verse 22 he counts himself among them ("we").

decisions.choice: Jews and Samaritans: two peoples long divided
decisions.reason: The Samaritans worshiped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but had their own temple on Mount Gerizim (verse 20). Jewish tradition traced them to the peoples the Assyrians settled in the land (2 Kings 17:24-41). The Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the Gerizim temple late in the second century BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.255-256), and the hostility between the two peoples ran deep (Luke 9:52-53).

decisions.choice: two barriers: Jew and Samaritan, man and woman
decisions.reason: The two participles set what he is against what she is, and she names herself a woman as well as a Samaritan. Verse 27 shows that a man talking with a woman in public also surprised the disciples.

decisions.choice: two statements, then the question
decisions.reason: Readable sets out the two facts first, so that the reason for her surprise is clear.

records.source: οὐ γὰρ συγχρῶνται Ἰουδαῖοι Σαμαρίταις.
records.gloss: Not for associate Jews with Samaritans.

L.9: For Jews do not use [things] in common with Samaritans.

R.9: (Jews do not share a cup or a bowl with Samaritans.)

decisions.choice: do not use things in common with: they do not share vessels
alternatives: have no dealings with, do not associate with
decisions.reason: The verb συγχρῶνται is rare. Formed from "with" and "use", it can mean to use something together with someone, and more broadly to have dealings with them. The broad sense sits awkwardly with verse 8, where the disciples go to buy food in a Samaritan town. The narrow sense suits the scene: Jesus has no vessel (verse 11) and would drink from hers, and a later Jewish ruling treated Samaritan women as always unclean, and so what they handled (Mishnah Niddah 4:1). The broader sense remains possible and is widely known; the footnote gives it.

decisions.choice: the narrator's comment, not the woman's words
decisions.reason: The sentence explains a custom for readers who did not know it, as John explains other Jewish customs (2:6). It stands outside her words.

decisions.choice: Jews: the Jewish people
decisions.reason: The word means the people as a whole, set beside the Samaritans as a people.

decisions.choice: the sentence is part of the text (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the sentence is missing (the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts)
decisions.reason: A few manuscripts leave the sentence out, perhaps because it seemed to contradict verse 8; the great majority have it. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: in parentheses
decisions.reason: Marks the sentence as the narrator's aside (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: use [things] in common (L); use the same vessels (B); share a cup or a bowl (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the shape of the verb; Balanced and Readable name what was not shared (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: Jews
decisions.reason: The word means the people here, so every level says "Jews" (see the book's terms).

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ· Εἰ ᾔδεις τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τίς ἐστιν ὁ λέγων σοι· Δός μοι πεῖν, σὺ ἂν ᾔτησας αὐτὸν καὶ ἔδωκεν ἄν σοι ὕδωρ ζῶν.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to her, "If you had known the gift of the God, and who is the one saying to you, 'Give me to drink,' you would have asked him and he would have given to you water living."

L.10: Jesus answered and said to her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, 'Give {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} [something] to drink,' you would have asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would have given you living water."

R.10: Jesus answered, "You do not know what God wants to give you. And you do not know who is asking you for a drink. If you did, you would have asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for water, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would have given you living water."

decisions.choice: an unreal condition with the roles reversed
decisions.reason: She does not know, and so she has not asked. The "you" in "you would have asked" is emphatic (σὺ): he asked her for water, but she is the one who should be asking him.

decisions.choice: the gift of God: what God freely gives, which the sentence names as living water
decisions.reason: δωρεὰν means a free gift. The sentence links God's gift with the living water Jesus would give; in 7:37-39 John explains living water as the Spirit, and in 3:16 God gives his Son. These belong together, so every level says only God's gift.

decisions.choice: living water: both fresh flowing water and water that gives life
alternatives: only a picture of eternal life
decisions.reason: In everyday speech living water was fresh water running from a spring or stream, as against still water in a cistern (Genesis 26:19; Leviticus 14:5, 50). Scripture also calls the LORD "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13), and the prophets see living water flowing out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8; Ezekiel 47:1-12). Jesus means the water of life that he gives; the woman hears the everyday sense (verse 11). The double meaning is deliberate, so every level keeps "living water".

decisions.choice: who it is: Jesus speaks of himself in the third person
decisions.reason: He points her to the question of who he is, which the conversation answers step by step: a Jew (verse 9), greater than Jacob (verse 12), a prophet (verse 19), the Messiah (verse 26).

decisions.choice: the gift God gives (B); what God wants to give you (R)
decisions.reason: Plain wording that keeps the gift open (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: it is you who would have asked him
decisions.reason: Shows the emphatic "you" (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: two statements, then the condition
decisions.reason: Readable states what she does not know before saying what would follow if she did.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ἡ γυνή· Κύριε, οὔτε ἄντλημα ἔχεις καὶ τὸ φρέαρ ἐστὶν βαθύ· πόθεν οὖν ἔχεις τὸ ὕδωρ τὸ ζῶν;
records.gloss: Says to him the woman, "Sir, neither a bucket you have, and the well is deep; from where then have you the water the living?"

L.11: The woman says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Sir, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep; from where then do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have the living water?

R.11: The woman said, "Sir, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do not have a bucket, and the well is deep. So how can {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} get this living water?

decisions.choice: Sir: a polite address to a man she does not know
decisions.reason: Κύριε is the word later used of Jesus as Lord (20:28), but it was also the ordinary courteous way to address a man. She does not yet know who he is. As the talk goes on she sees him as a prophet (verse 19) and wonders if he is the Christ (verse 29).

decisions.choice: bucket: a vessel for drawing water
decisions.reason: The word means something to draw water with, such as a bucket let down on a rope. Jesus has none.

decisions.choice: she takes living water in the everyday sense
decisions.reason: She thinks of running water and sees that he cannot even reach the water in this well, let alone a better source. John often lets hearers take Jesus's words at the everyday level before their meaning is opened (3:4; 4:33; 6:52).

decisions.choice: well: a shaft dug down to water
decisions.reason: A different word from the "spring" of verse 6; see the note there.

decisions.choice: Sir
decisions.reason: The woman uses the word as a polite address (meaning decision m1); "Lord" would put in her mouth a confession she has not yet made. The footnote gives "Lord", the other sense of the same Greek word.

records.source: μὴ σὺ μείζων εἶ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἰακώβ, ὃς ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν τὸ φρέαρ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἔπιεν καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ θρέμματα αὐτοῦ;
records.gloss: Not you greater are than the father of us Jacob, who gave us the well, and himself from it drank and the sons of him and the livestock of him?

L.12: Surely {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are not greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and drank from it himself, and his sons and his livestock?"

R.12: Our ancestor Jacob gave us this well. He drank from it, and so did his sons and his animals. Do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} think {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are greater than Jacob?"

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The question is framed to expect "no". John's readers know the answer is yes; the same irony returns when the crowd asks whether Jesus is greater than Abraham (8:53).

decisions.choice: our father Jacob: the Samaritans claimed descent from Jacob through Joseph
decisions.reason: Josephus reports that the Samaritans called themselves descendants of Joseph through Ephraim and Manasseh (Antiquities 11.341). The well that Jacob gave stands for that claim.

decisions.choice: livestock: flocks and herds
decisions.reason: The word covers the animals a household raised and kept.

decisions.choice: ancestor
decisions.reason: Jacob lived long before; "father" in this sense is not plain for young readers.

decisions.choice: the question first (B) or last (R), with Jacob's gift as its own sentence
decisions.reason: Breaks the long question so it reads naturally; Readable's "Do you think" keeps the expected answer no (meaning decision m1).

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ· Πᾶς ὁ πίνων ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος τούτου διψήσει πάλιν·
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to her, "Everyone drinking of the water this will thirst again;

L.13: Jesus answered and said to her, "{{gender:Everyone|Every man}} who drinks of this water will thirst again;

R.13: Jesus answered, "{{gender:Anyone|Any man}} who drinks this water will get thirsty again.

decisions.choice: everyone who drinks: anyone at all, and drinking again and again
decisions.reason: The masculine is the general form and includes the woman herself. The present participle describes ordinary drinking, done over and over; verse 14 sets against it a single drink of what Jesus gives.

decisions.choice: this water: the water of Jacob's well
decisions.reason: The water she came to draw, which she has just praised as Jacob's gift.

decisions.choice: {{gender:Everyone|Every man}} (L); {{gender:All who|All men who}} (B); {{gender:Anyone|Any man}} (R)
alternatives: Everyone at every level, with no setting
decisions.reason: Inclusive by default, since men and women are meant; the traditional form is the alternative.

records.source: ὃς δ’ ἂν πίῃ ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος οὗ ἐγὼ δώσω αὐτῷ, οὐ μὴ διψήσει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, ἀλλὰ τὸ ὕδωρ ὃ δώσω αὐτῷ γενήσεται ἐν αὐτῷ πηγὴ ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: whoever however may drink of the water that I will give him, never not will thirst into the age, but the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into life eternal."

L.14: But whoever drinks of the water that I will give {{gender:them|him}} will never, ever thirst; rather, the water that I will give {{gender:them|him}} will become in {{gender:them|him}} a spring of water leaping up into eternal life."

R.14: But the water I give is different. {{gender:Anyone|Any man}} who drinks it will not get thirsty again, not ever. It will become like a spring inside {{gender:them|him}}. Its water will bubble up and bring {{gender:them|him}} eternal life, the life of the age to come, which starts now."

decisions.choice: never, ever: the strongest denial, with "for ever"
decisions.reason: Two negatives together (οὐ μὴ) make the strongest denial, and "into the age" adds "for ever". The thirst that ordinary water only puts off, this water ends.

decisions.choice: whoever drinks: a single drink
decisions.reason: The aorist subjunctive looks at one act of drinking, set against the repeated drinking of verse 13.

decisions.choice: the water Jesus gives: the life he gives, which John later links with the Spirit
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say here what the water is. In 7:37-39 he promises rivers of living water flowing from within the one who believes, and John explains that he meant the Spirit. Isaiah promised water for the thirsty and the Spirit poured out (Isaiah 44:3; 55:1). Here the water becomes a source inside the person, no longer drawn from outside.

decisions.choice: leaping up: water gushing up from a spring
decisions.reason: The verb ἁλλομένου is used elsewhere of people jumping or leaping (Acts 3:8; 14:10). Used of water, it pictures a spring gushing up with force: water that is alive.

decisions.choice: into eternal life: the water rises and issues in eternal life
decisions.reason: The phrase gives the direction and goal of the water: it leads to eternal life. The same phrase is used of the harvest gathered "for eternal life" in verse 36.

decisions.choice: eternal life: the life of the age to come, which begins now
decisions.reason: In John eternal life is the life of God's coming age, given now to those who believe (3:15-16, 36; 5:24).

decisions.choice: leaping up (L); leaps up (B); bubble up (R)
decisions.reason: The verb is used of jumping (meaning decision m4); "leaping" keeps that lively picture, which the more familiar renderings soften. Readable uses the plain word for water rising from a spring.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}; {{gender:Anyone|Any man}}
decisions.reason: "Whoever" means men and women; inclusive by default, the traditional form as the alternative.

decisions.choice: the life of the age to come, which starts now
decisions.reason: The book-wide explanation of eternal life, given once in this passage (meaning decision m6).

decisions.choice: never, ever
decisions.reason: One phrase that carries both the double negative and "into the age" (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: But the water I give is different.
decisions.reason: Readable sets up the contrast with verse 13 before stating it.

records.source: λέγει πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡ γυνή· Κύριε, δός μοι τοῦτο τὸ ὕδωρ, ἵνα μὴ διψῶ μηδὲ διέρχωμαι ἐνθάδε ἀντλεῖν.
records.gloss: Says to him the woman, "Sir, give me this the water, so that not I may thirst nor come through here to draw."

L.15: The woman says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Sir, give me this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come all the way here to draw [water]."

R.15: The woman said, "Sir, give me this water! Then I will not get thirsty, and I will not have to walk all the way here to get water."

decisions.choice: she asks, still thinking of ordinary water
decisions.reason: She takes up his words at the everyday level: water that would end thirst and the daily walk to the well. Whether she speaks in earnest or half in jest the text does not say, and every level gives her words without tone. Jesus's answer turns the talk to her own life.

decisions.choice: come all the way here
decisions.reason: The verb means to come through or come all the way, hinting at the distance from the town (verse 5). It is the verb used of Jesus passing through Samaria in verse 4.

decisions.choice: be spared the trip out here (B); walk all the way here (R)
decisions.reason: Shows the distance the verb suggests (meaning decision m2).

records.source: Λέγει αὐτῇ· Ὕπαγε φώνησον τὸν ἄνδρα σου καὶ ἐλθὲ ἐνθάδε.
records.gloss: He says to her, "Go, call the husband of you and come here."

L.16: He says to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here."

R.16: Jesus told her, "Go and get your husband. Then come back here."

decisions.choice: husband: the same word means "man" and "husband"
decisions.reason: ἄνδρα is both the ordinary word for a man and the word for a husband. Verses 17-18 turn on this: the man she has now is not her husband.

decisions.choice: Jesus turns the talk to her life
decisions.reason: He already knows the answer (verse 18; compare 2:25). The request leads her to the truth about herself, and from there to who he is (verses 19, 29).

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη ἡ γυνὴ καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Οὐκ ἔχω ἄνδρα.
records.gloss: Answered the woman and said to him, "Not I have a husband."

L.17: The woman answered and said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "I do not have a husband."

R.17: The woman answered, "I do not have a husband."

decisions.choice: true in its words, but not the whole truth
decisions.reason: What she says is true, as Jesus grants, but it hides what he goes on to name.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Καλῶς εἶπας ὅτι Ἄνδρα οὐκ ἔχω·
records.gloss: Says to her the Jesus, "Well you said, 'A husband not I have';

L.17: Jesus says to her, "You said well, 'A husband I do not have';

R.17: Jesus said to her, "You are right when you say you do not have a husband.

decisions.choice: well: rightly, truly
decisions.reason: The adverb grants that her words are correct; in the light of verse 18 it is said with gentle irony.

decisions.choice: husband placed first
decisions.reason: As Jesus repeats her words, "husband" moves to the front: that is the very word he takes up.

decisions.choice: A husband I do not have
alternatives: I do not have a husband
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek order, which stresses the word (meaning decision m2).

records.source: πέντε γὰρ ἄνδρας ἔσχες, καὶ νῦν ὃν ἔχεις οὐκ ἔστιν σου ἀνήρ· τοῦτο ἀληθὲς εἴρηκας.
records.gloss: five for husbands you had, and now whom you have not is your husband; this true you have spoken."

L.18: For five husbands you have had, and the one you now have is not your husband; this you have said truly."

R.18: You have had five husbands, and the man you are living with now is not your husband. You told the truth."

decisions.choice: five husbands: John gives the fact without explaining it
alternatives: a sign of a sinful life
a picture of the five peoples settled in Samaria (2 Kings 17:24)
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say why she had had five husbands. Under the law a husband could end a marriage but a wife could not (Deuteronomy 24:1-4), and a woman could be widowed more than once, so the number alone does not show whose fault it was. John records no rebuke; what amazes her is that he knows (verse 29). Some have read the five husbands as a picture of the five peoples the Assyrians settled in Samaria with their gods (2 Kings 17:24, 29-31); John gives no sign of it.

decisions.choice: the one you have now is not your husband: she lives with a man she is not married to
decisions.reason: "Have" is used as in "have a husband" (verse 17); the present man is not her husband by marriage.

decisions.choice: this you have said truly: what she said matches the facts
decisions.reason: "This" stands first: in this, at least, she spoke the truth, though she did not say all of it.

decisions.choice: Jesus knows her life
decisions.reason: As with Nathanael (1:47-48), Jesus knows what is in a person (2:25). She will tell the town, "He told me everything I ever did" (verse 29).

decisions.choice: In fact
decisions.reason: The Greek "for" gives the reason her words were right; "in fact" does the same in natural speech.

decisions.choice: the one you are with now (B); the man you are living with now (R)
decisions.reason: Says plainly what "have" means here (meaning decision m2).

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ἡ γυνή· Κύριε, θεωρῶ ὅτι προφήτης εἶ σύ.
records.gloss: Says to him the woman, "Sir, I perceive that a prophet are you.

L.19: The woman says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Sir, I perceive that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are a prophet.

R.19: The woman said, "Sir, I can tell that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are a prophet.

decisions.choice: I perceive: she has come to see it
decisions.reason: The verb means to look at and so to realize; his knowledge of her life has led her to this.

decisions.choice: a prophet: one through whom God speaks and who may know what is hidden
decisions.reason: Prophets were known for seeing what was hidden (1 Samuel 9:19-20; 2 Kings 5:26; compare Luke 7:39). There is no article, so she does not yet call him "the Prophet" (1:21; 6:14). The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture and looked for the prophet like Moses whom God had promised (Deuteronomy 18:15-18); her words point that way (verse 25).

records.source: οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ ὄρει τούτῳ προσεκύνησαν· καὶ ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐστὶν ὁ τόπος ὅπου προσκυνεῖν δεῖ.
records.gloss: The fathers of us on the mountain this worshiped; and you say that in Jerusalem is the place where to worship it is necessary."

L.20: Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you [Jews] say that in Jerusalem is the place where [people] must worship."

R.20: Our ancestors worshiped God here on this mountain. But you Jews say that people must worship in Jerusalem."

decisions.choice: this mountain: Mount Gerizim, above the well
decisions.reason: Mount Gerizim rises over the valley where the well lies. Moses commanded the blessing to be spoken from Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12), and in the Samaritan form of the five books of Moses the altar of Deuteronomy 27:4 is on Gerizim, where the Jewish text has Mount Ebal. The Samaritans' temple there was destroyed late in the second century BC (see verse 9), but they went on worshiping on the mountain.

decisions.choice: our fathers: the Samaritans' ancestors, back to the patriarchs
decisions.reason: Abraham and Jacob built altars near Shechem (Genesis 12:6-7; 33:18-20). She appeals to her people's long tradition.

decisions.choice: you: plural, the Jews
decisions.reason: She sets "our fathers" against "you" in the plural: the Jews, whose view she takes this Jewish prophet to share.

decisions.choice: must: a duty laid down by God
decisions.reason: The Jewish claim rested on the command to worship at the place God would choose (Deuteronomy 12:5-14), which Scripture names as Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 6:6; Psalm 78:68). Jesus answers in verse 24 with a different "must".

decisions.choice: a question put to a prophet
alternatives: only a way of changing the subject
decisions.reason: Having found a prophet, she raises the question that divided the two peoples. Whether she is also turning the talk away from her own life the text does not say.

decisions.choice: you [Jews] (L); you Jews (B, R)
decisions.reason: The plural "you" (meaning decision m3) needs a word to show it. It refers to the Jews as a people, so it does not take the setting for pronouns of Christ.

decisions.choice: ancestors
decisions.reason: "Fathers" here means forebears; "ancestors" says so plainly.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Πίστευέ μοι, γύναι, ὅτι ἔρχεται ὥρα ὅτε οὔτε ἐν τῷ ὄρει τούτῳ οὔτε ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις προσκυνήσετε τῷ πατρί.
records.gloss: Says to her the Jesus, "Believe me, woman, that is coming an hour when neither on the mountain this nor in Jerusalem you will worship the Father.

L.21: Jesus says to her, "Believe {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, Woman, that an hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you [all] worship the Father.

R.21: Jesus said to her, "Dear woman, believe {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. A time is coming when you and your people will worship the Father, but not on this mountain, and not in Jerusalem either.

decisions.choice: an hour is coming: the time God has set, which begins with Jesus
decisions.reason: As with Jesus's hour (2:4), this is a time set by God. Verse 23 adds "and now is": with Jesus it has already begun. His body is the new temple (2:19-21), so worship will no longer be bound to a place.

decisions.choice: Woman: a respectful address
decisions.reason: See the note at 2:4. Jesus speaks to her with the same courtesy he shows his mother.

decisions.choice: you will worship: plural, the woman and her people
decisions.reason: The verb is plural. Jesus speaks of a time when her people will worship the Father, neither at Gerizim nor at Jerusalem but in the way verses 23-24 describe. Verses 39-42 begin to fulfil it.

decisions.choice: the Father: Jesus speaks of God as Father
decisions.reason: From here to verse 23 Jesus calls God "the Father": true worship is worship of the Father whom the Son makes known (1:18).

decisions.choice: believe me: trust what I say
decisions.reason: With a plain object rather than "in", the verb means to accept what someone says as true.

decisions.choice: Woman
decisions.reason: As at 2:4: "Woman" on its own can sound cold, but keeping it lets readers connect the passages; the footnote says it was respectful.

decisions.choice: Dear woman
decisions.reason: For young readers "Woman" sounds rude, which the Greek is not; "Dear woman" keeps the courtesy (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: A time
decisions.reason: "Hour" sounds like sixty minutes; Literal and Balanced keep "hour" so the thread through the Gospel stays visible.

decisions.choice: you [all] (L); your worship (B); you and your people (R)
decisions.reason: Shows that "you" is plural (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: your worship of the Father will not be on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem either
alternatives: you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Natural word order that keeps the stress on the two places.

records.source: ὑμεῖς προσκυνεῖτε ὃ οὐκ οἴδατε, ἡμεῖς προσκυνοῦμεν ὃ οἴδαμεν, ὅτι ἡ σωτηρία ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐστίν·
records.gloss: You worship what not you know; we worship what we know, because the salvation from the Jews is;

L.22: You [all] worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews.

R.22: You Samaritans do not really know the God you worship. We Jews know the God we worship, because God's salvation comes from the Jewish people.

decisions.choice: you (plural): the Samaritans; we: the Jews, among whom Jesus counts himself
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks as a Jew to a Samaritan, taking up her "our fathers" and "you" (verse 20).

decisions.choice: what: worship that does not truly know its object
decisions.reason: The neuter "what" rather than "whom" suggests worship without full knowledge of the God it is offered to. The Samaritans accepted the books of Moses but not the Prophets, and 2 Kings 17:33 describes the settlers as fearing the LORD while serving their own gods. Jesus's "we know" rests on what God made known to Israel.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people
decisions.reason: Here the word clearly means the Jewish people, and Jesus speaks as one of them.

decisions.choice: salvation is from the Jews: God's saving work comes through Israel
decisions.reason: God's promises were given to Israel for all nations (Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 2:3), and the Christ comes from Israel by descent (Romans 9:4-5). The Samaritans of Sychar will call Jesus "the Savior of the world" (verse 42).

decisions.choice: Your people (B); You Samaritans, We Jews (R)
decisions.reason: Shows who "you" and "we" are (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: the Jewish people
decisions.reason: The word means the people here (see the book's terms).

decisions.choice: the God you worship; the God we worship
decisions.reason: Readable names the one worshiped; "not really" keeps the sense of the neuter (meaning decision m2).

records.source: ἀλλὰ ἔρχεται ὥρα καὶ νῦν ἐστιν, ὅτε οἱ ἀληθινοὶ προσκυνηταὶ προσκυνήσουσιν τῷ πατρὶ ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ, καὶ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ τοιούτους ζητεῖ τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας αὐτόν·
records.gloss: But is coming an hour and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for also the Father such seeks the ones worshiping him;

L.23: But an hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for indeed the Father seeks such [{{gender:people|men}}] as those who worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.23: But a time is coming, and it has already started, when those who truly worship the Father will worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in spirit and in truth. The Father is looking for {{gender:people|men}} who will worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} like that.

decisions.choice: is coming and now is: the future time is already present in Jesus
decisions.reason: The hour still lies ahead, but with Jesus present it has already begun. John says the same of the hour when the dead hear the voice of the Son of God (5:25).

decisions.choice: true: genuine, real
decisions.reason: ἀληθινοὶ means real or genuine, as in "the true light" (1:9) and "the true vine" (15:1).

decisions.choice: in spirit and truth: one idea, worship that fits who God is (spirit, verse 24) and the truth he has made known; spirit is not capitalized
alternatives: in the Spirit and in truth: worship given through the Holy Spirit
in one's inner spirit, sincerely, as against outward ritual
decisions.reason: One preposition governs both nouns, so they form a single idea. Verse 24 grounds it: God is spirit, so worship must be "in spirit". The word could refer to the Holy Spirit, whom John links with new birth (3:5-8) and calls "the Spirit of truth" (14:17; 15:26), and through whom such worship becomes possible. But the sentence describes the kind of worship rather than naming the Spirit, and verse 24 uses the same word of God's own being, so it is not capitalized here. It is not mere inward sincerity either, since it is joined to truth. The evidence is balanced; the footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: truth: the reality of God made known in Jesus
decisions.reason: In John truth is God's reality made known: grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (1:17), and he is the truth (14:6). True worship is shaped by that truth, not only offered sincerely.

decisions.choice: the Father seeks such people as his worshipers: God takes the first step
decisions.reason: Word for word, "the Father seeks such [people as] those who worship him": the participle says what he seeks them to be. The masculine is general and includes men and women. Worship begins with God's seeking, as the shepherd seeks the lost (Ezekiel 34:11-12; Luke 19:10); at the well Jesus has been doing just that.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: Men and women are meant; inclusive by default, the traditional form as the alternative.

decisions.choice: it has already begun (B); it has already started (R)
decisions.reason: Plain words for the hour's present arrival (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: a time
decisions.reason: As in verse 21.

records.source: πνεῦμα ὁ θεός, καὶ τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας αὐτὸν ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν.
records.gloss: Spirit the God [is], and the ones worshiping him in spirit and truth it is necessary to worship."

L.24: God [is] spirit, and it is necessary for those who worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to worship in spirit and truth."

R.24: God is spirit. So when people worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they need to worship in spirit and in truth."

decisions.choice: God is spirit: what God is, not "a spirit" and not the Holy Spirit
alternatives: God is a spirit, one among many
decisions.reason: πνεῦμα stands first without the article and describes God's nature, like "God is light" (1 John 1:5) and "God is love" (1 John 4:8). God is not bound to a body or a place, so he cannot be confined to one mountain or one city (compare 1 Kings 8:27). Since it describes God's being and does not name the Holy Spirit, the book-wide choice is not to capitalize it.

decisions.choice: must: a necessity that comes from who God is
decisions.reason: The woman spoke of the place where people "must" worship (verse 20). Jesus answers with a "must" that rests on God's own nature, not on a place.

decisions.choice: in spirit and truth: as in verse 23
alternatives: in the Spirit and in truth
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m3 at verse 23, whose footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: those who worship him: men and women alike
decisions.reason: The masculine plural participle is general.

decisions.choice: it is necessary for those who worship him to worship
alternatives: those who worship him must worship
decisions.reason: Keeps the Greek shape, with the necessity stated before the worship it governs.

decisions.choice: anyone who worships him (B); when people worship him (R)
decisions.reason: Plain words that include men and women without needing the gender setting.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ἡ γυνή· Οἶδα ὅτι Μεσσίας ἔρχεται, ὁ λεγόμενος χριστός· ὅταν ἔλθῃ ἐκεῖνος, ἀναγγελεῖ ἡμῖν ἅπαντα.
records.gloss: Says to him the woman, "I know that Messiah is coming" (the one being called Christ); "when comes that one, he will declare to us all things."

L.25: The woman says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "I know that Messiah is coming" (who is called {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}); "when that one comes, [{{deity_pronoun:he|He}}] will declare all things to us."

R.25: The woman said, "I know that the Messiah is coming." (Messiah means the {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}, the one God promised to send.) "When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will explain everything to us."

decisions.choice: Messiah: the Hebrew title in Greek letters, which John translates
decisions.reason: As at 1:41, the word Μεσσίας is the Hebrew (and Aramaic) title, anointed one, written in Greek letters and then translated with χριστός. The woman uses it without the article, almost as a name.

decisions.choice: who is called Christ: most likely the narrator's explanation
decisions.reason: At 1:38, 1:41 and 1:42 John stops to translate a Hebrew or Aramaic word for his readers, and this phrase does the same, so it is set outside her words. The manuscripts have no quotation marks, though, and the words can be read as hers.

decisions.choice: the Samaritan hope: a coming one who would teach the truth
decisions.reason: The Samaritans drew their hope from the five books of Moses, especially the prophet like Moses who would tell the people all that God commanded (Deuteronomy 18:18). Her words "he will declare all things to us" fit that hope. Later Samaritan writings call the coming one the Taheb, "the one who returns"; how much of that belief goes back to Jesus's day is not certain.

decisions.choice: declare: make known, report
decisions.reason: She expects the coming one to settle questions like the one she raised about worship (verse 20). The same verb is used of the Spirit, who "will declare" to the disciples what is to come (16:13-15).

decisions.choice: Messiah, plain; {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}} for the explanation
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for 1:41 and 4:25: Messiah is the woman's word and is written plainly. The christos setting is on the explanation only, with "Anointed One" as its alternative, so no setting can produce "Messiah (who is called Messiah)".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} for the coming one
decisions.reason: The one she speaks of is Christ, so the pronouns for him take the setting, though she does not yet know who he is. Literal brackets the "he" that the verb contains.

decisions.choice: Messiah means the Anointed One, the one God promised to send
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title (meaning decisions m1 and m3) without making it the king of David's line, which was the Jewish rather than the Samaritan hope.

decisions.choice: make everything plain (B); explain everything (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday words for what she expects (meaning decision m4).

records.source: λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ λαλῶν σοι.
records.gloss: Says to her the Jesus, "I am, the one speaking to you."

L.26: Jesus says to her, "I am [{{deity_pronoun:he|He}}], the one speaking to you."

R.26: Jesus told her, "I am the Messiah, the one who is talking to you."

decisions.choice: I am: plainly "I am he", the Messiah, with a possible echo of God's own words
alternatives: the divine name, I AM, as the main sense
only the plain sense, with no echo
decisions.reason: The words Ἐγώ εἰμι have no predicate, but the woman has just spoken of Messiah, so the plain sense is "I am he": Jesus says openly what he is, as he does to no one else so plainly before his trial (compare 10:24-25). The same words are how God speaks of himself in the Greek of Isaiah (43:10; 46:4), and in Isaiah 52:6 God says, "I am he who is speaking", very like the wording here. Later in John the bare "I am" carries that echo more clearly (8:24, 28, 58). Here the plain sense is uppermost and the echo possible, so the decision is marked uncertain.

decisions.choice: the one speaking to you: the one she awaits is already here
decisions.reason: She spoke of one who will come and declare all things; the one now declaring things to her is he. The conversation that began with his request for water ends with his naming himself.

decisions.choice: I am [he] (L); I am he (B)
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "I am". Literal brackets the "he" the sentence needs; Balanced writes it. As a pronoun for Christ it takes the deity_pronoun setting. The footnote gives the bare words, so the echo noted in meaning decision m1 stays visible.

decisions.choice: I am the Messiah
decisions.reason: Readable says whom "he" refers to (verse 25).

records.source: Καὶ ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἦλθαν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐθαύμαζον ὅτι μετὰ γυναικὸς ἐλάλει· οὐδεὶς μέντοι εἶπεν· Τί ζητεῖς;
records.gloss: And upon this came the disciples of him, and they were marveling that with a woman he was speaking; no one however said, "What do you seek?"

L.27: And at this [moment] {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples came, and they were marveling that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, "What are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} seeking?"

R.27: Right then Jesus's disciples came back. They were amazed that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was talking with a woman. But none of them asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "What do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} want from her?"

decisions.choice: at this: just as Jesus said "I am he" (4:26)
decisions.reason: The phrase marks the moment. The disciples, who had gone into the town to buy food (4:8), come back at the very point where Jesus has told the woman who he is, and the conversation ends.

decisions.choice: they were surprised that a teacher was talking in public with a woman
alternatives: surprised only that she was a Samaritan
decisions.reason: John says "a woman", not "a Samaritan": the surprise is that a teacher was talking alone with a woman he did not know. Jewish teaching of the time was wary of this; the Mishnah, collected about AD 200, records the saying "do not talk much with a woman" (Avot 1:5). That she was also a Samaritan (4:9) made it stranger still. The imperfect verb pictures their surprise as lasting while they took in the scene.

decisions.choice: both questions are ones they might have put to Jesus, and did not
alternatives: the first question is to the woman (what do you want?), the second to Jesus
decisions.reason: The verbs are singular, and the second question, "why are you speaking with her?", is plainly to Jesus; joined by "or", the two are most naturally alternatives put to the same person. μέντοι ("yet") shows that respect for their teacher kept them quiet. "What are you seeking?" is the question Jesus himself asked the first disciples (1:38).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "you" when people speak to him, as here, even though the question is not spoken aloud. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: What are you looking for? (B); What do you want from her? (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the same everyday words as at 1:38, so the echo stays visible; Readable says plainly what the question would have meant here and supplies "from her", which the scene implies.

records.source: ἢ τί λαλεῖς μετ’ αὐτῆς;
records.gloss: Or why do you speak with her?

decisions.choice: a second question, its own sentence in the SBLGNT but still governed by "no one said"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the first question with a question mark and begins this one with "or", so the record starts in the middle of the reported speech. Both questions belong to what the disciples did not say; the renderings begin in lower case so that the two records read as one sentence.

records.source: ἀφῆκεν οὖν τὴν ὑδρίαν αὐτῆς ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὴν πόλιν καὶ λέγει τοῖς ἀνθρώποις·
records.gloss: Left then the water jar of her the woman and went away into the city and says to the people:

L.28: So the woman left her water jar and went away into the town, and she says to the {{gender:people|men}},

R.28: The woman left her water jar there and hurried back to the town. She said to the {{gender:people|men}} there,

decisions.choice: she left the jar behind as she went off to the town
alternatives: a deliberate sign that she no longer cares for well water (4:13-15)
decisions.reason: She came to draw water (4:7), and now she leaves the jar at the well, perhaps in haste and meaning to come back. Some readers see a picture in it: she has found the living water Jesus spoke of (4:10-14). John does not say so, so every level simply reports it.

decisions.choice: the town: Sychar (4:5)
decisions.reason: The word is used of any walled or settled place, small or large. Here it is Sychar, the town near Jacob's well (4:5).

decisions.choice: the people of the town, men and women
alternatives: only the men, gathered in a public place
decisions.reason: The plural of this word is the ordinary term for people in general; it does not mark them as male. Those she speaks to are the townspeople who then come out (4:30) and of whom many believe (4:39-42).

decisions.choice: the {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The word means people in general (meaning decision m3), so the inclusive word is the default and the gender setting gives the traditional "men".

decisions.choice: said
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("she says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage.

decisions.choice: town
decisions.reason: Sychar was a small place (meaning decision m2); "city" would suggest something much larger.

decisions.choice: hurried back
decisions.reason: Readable shows the haste implied by her leaving the jar and going at once.

records.source: Δεῦτε ἴδετε ἄνθρωπον ὃς εἶπέ μοι πάντα ὅσα ἐποίησα· μήτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ χριστός;
records.gloss: "Come, see a man who told me all things as many as I did; can it be that this one is the Christ?"

L.29: "Come, see a man who told me all the things that I did. Can it be that this [man] is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?"

R.29: "Come and see a man who told me all the things I have ever done! Might {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} be the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?"

decisions.choice: everything I have done: an overstatement that sums up her life
alternatives: a full list of her deeds
decisions.reason: Jesus had told her about her five husbands and the man she now lived with (4:16-18). That he knew this was enough to show he knew her whole life. Her words also echo what she said of the Messiah: "he will tell us all things" (4:25).

decisions.choice: a hesitant question that hopes but does not claim: could this be the Christ?
alternatives: a question expecting yes: is not this the Christ?
a question expecting no: this cannot be the Christ
decisions.reason: μήτι normally introduces a question that expects "no" (as in 4:33). Here, as in Matthew 12:23, it voices a guarded hope: she does not dare to assert it, but she raises it so that others will come and judge for themselves. The renderings keep the question tentative. Some older versions turned it into a confident "Is not this the Christ?", which the form does not support.

decisions.choice: the Christ: the title, the Anointed One she has just spoken of (4:25)
decisions.reason: With the article the word is a title. The woman herself used the Hebrew word Messiah, which John translates (4:25). Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses, and their hope rested on the promise of a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15-18); later Samaritan writings speak of a coming restorer who would reveal the truth.

decisions.choice: Come, see: she invites others as Philip invited Nathanael
decisions.reason: The two plural commands repeat the pattern of 1:39 and 1:46, "come and see": the one who has met Jesus brings others to see for themselves. The woman becomes the first witness to Jesus in Samaria (4:39).

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: A title with the article, so every level writes "the" outside the span, as at 1:20.

decisions.choice: Could this possibly be ...? (B); Might he be ...? (R)
alternatives: He cannot be the Christ, can he?
decisions.reason: These keep the hesitation of the question (meaning decision m2) without turning it into a denial or a confession.

records.source: ἐξῆλθον ἐκ τῆς πόλεως καὶ ἤρχοντο πρὸς αὐτόν.
records.gloss: They went out from the city and were coming toward him.

L.30: They went out of the town and were coming to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.30: So the people left the town and started out toward Jesus.

decisions.choice: they set out, and were on their way while Jesus spoke with his disciples
decisions.reason: The first verb tells of the setting out, the second (an imperfect) of a journey still going on. John leaves them coming across the fields during 4:31-38 and brings them to Jesus at 4:40. The harvest Jesus speaks of is coming toward him as he speaks.

decisions.choice: no connecting word (SBLGNT)
alternatives: "so they went out" (many later manuscripts add a connecting word)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add a word for "so" or "then", as the King James Version reflects. The sense is the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: The people (B, R); Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject, the townspeople of 4:28; Readable also names Jesus.

decisions.choice: began making their way (B); started out toward (R)
decisions.reason: Shows that they were still on the way (meaning decision m1).

records.source: Ἐν τῷ μεταξὺ ἠρώτων αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταὶ λέγοντες· Ῥαββί, φάγε.
records.gloss: In the meantime were asking him the disciples saying, "Rabbi, eat."

L.31: In the meantime the disciples were urging {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Rabbi, eat."

R.31: While this was happening, the disciples kept saying to Jesus, "Rabbi, please eat something."

decisions.choice: were urging him: kept asking him to eat
decisions.reason: The verb usually means "ask", and it can mean a request as well as a question. Here what follows is a request, and the imperfect shows them pressing it more than once.

decisions.choice: Rabbi: the respectful title for a teacher
decisions.reason: The disciples use the title John explained at 1:38. They had gone to the town for food (4:8) and now offer it to him.

decisions.choice: Rabbi
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: John translates the word himself (1:38), so every level keeps it.

decisions.choice: something (B, R); please (R)
decisions.reason: A bare "eat" sounds abrupt; the words give the friendly tone of the disciples' request.

records.heading: Fields ready for harvest

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ἐγὼ βρῶσιν ἔχω φαγεῖν ἣν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε.
records.gloss: But he said to them, "I food have to eat which you not know."

L.32: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know."

R.32: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "I have a kind of food that you do not know about."

decisions.choice: emphatic I and you: I have food; you do not know it
decisions.reason: Both pronouns are written out, which Greek does for emphasis: what sustains Jesus is something the disciples know nothing of.

decisions.choice: food in a sense beyond the literal, explained in verse 34
alternatives: Jesus has been given a meal
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of food as he spoke of water with the woman (4:10-15) and of the temple with the authorities (2:19-21): his hearers take him literally, and he then explains. The disciples misunderstand (4:33) just as the woman did.

decisions.choice: you do not know: you have no knowledge of it
decisions.reason: The verb is "know". They do not know that such food exists, nor what it is.

decisions.choice: you are not aware of (B); you do not know about (R)
decisions.reason: "Know" with "food" as its object is unnatural here; these say what it means (meaning decision m3).

records.source: ἔλεγον οὖν οἱ μαθηταὶ πρὸς ἀλλήλους· Μή τις ἤνεγκεν αὐτῷ φαγεῖν;
records.gloss: Were saying therefore the disciples to one another, "Not anyone brought him to eat?"

L.33: So the disciples were saying to one another, "No one brought {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [anything] to eat, did they?"

R.33: So the disciples asked each other, "Did someone bring {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} food while we were gone?"

decisions.choice: a puzzled question that expects no
decisions.reason: Μή at the head of the question expects the answer "no": they cannot think who would have fed him in Samaria (4:9), yet they can find no other explanation.

decisions.choice: they take his words about food literally
decisions.reason: Like the woman with the water (4:11), the disciples think of ordinary food. Their question prepares for Jesus's explanation in the next verse.

decisions.choice: Did someone bring him food while we were gone?
alternatives: No one brought him food, did they?
decisions.reason: Readable asks the question plainly and adds "while we were gone", which the story implies (4:8); the puzzled tone remains.

records.source: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐμὸν βρῶμά ἐστιν ἵνα ποιήσω τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πέμψαντός με καὶ τελειώσω αὐτοῦ τὸ ἔργον.
records.gloss: Says to them the Jesus, "My food is that I do the will of the one having sent me and complete his the work."

L.34: Jesus says to them, "My food is that I should do the will of the [one] who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and should complete {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} work."

R.34: Jesus said, "My food is to do what God wants. He sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} food is to finish {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} work."

decisions.choice: what sustains Jesus is doing the Father's will
decisions.reason: Food gives life and strength; Jesus says his life is fed by obedience. The thought is like Deuteronomy 8:3, that people do not live by bread alone. Later he says, "I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me" (6:38).

decisions.choice: the one who sent me: God the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus often describes God as "the one who sent me" (5:24, 30; 6:38-39; 7:16). It presents him as the Father's envoy, who speaks and acts for the one who sent him.

decisions.choice: complete: carry through to the end
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring something to its goal. Jesus uses it again in his prayer, "I have completed the work you gave me to do" (17:4), and from the cross he says "It is finished" (19:30), from the same root.

decisions.choice: doing ... bringing ... to completion
alternatives: that I should do ... and complete (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the purpose clause into a plain description of what his food is.

decisions.choice: what God wants. He sent me
alternatives: the will of the one who sent me
decisions.reason: Readable names God, whom "the one who sent me" means (meaning decision m2), and splits the long phrase into short sentences.

records.source: οὐχ ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι Ἔτι τετράμηνός ἐστιν καὶ ὁ θερισμὸς ἔρχεται;
records.gloss: Not you say that, "Yet four months it is and the harvest comes"?

L.35: "Do you not say, 'It is still four months, and the harvest comes'?

R.35: "You say, 'In four more months the harvest will come.'

decisions.choice: a common saying, or a remark on the season: either way, "the harvest is still far off"
alternatives: a saying about the time between sowing and harvest
a time note: the scene is four months before harvest, in winter
decisions.reason: The words have the shape of a saying, and "do you not say" points to something people often said; the gap between sowing and the grain harvest was about this long. But no such saying is known from elsewhere, and the words may be a plain remark about the time of year, which would place the scene in winter, some four months before the harvest in spring. Either way the point is the same: the disciples think the harvest is still to come, and Jesus says it is here now.

decisions.choice: emphatic you: you say this, but I tell you (next sentence)
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out, setting the disciples' saying against Jesus's own words that follow.

decisions.choice: You say
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes", so Readable states it plainly.

records.source: ἰδοὺ λέγω ὑμῖν, ἐπάρατε τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑμῶν καὶ θεάσασθε τὰς χώρας ὅτι λευκαί εἰσιν πρὸς θερισμόν· ἤδη ὁ θερίζων μισθὸν λαμβάνει καὶ συνάγει καρπὸν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, ἵνα ὁ σπείρων ὁμοῦ χαίρῃ καὶ ὁ θερίζων.
records.gloss: Look, I say to you, lift up the eyes of you and see the fields, that white they are toward harvest. \v 36 Already the one reaping a wage receives and gathers fruit into life eternal, so that the one sowing together may rejoice and the one reaping.

L.35: Look, I say to you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, that they are white for harvest.
L.36: Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that the one who sows and the one who reaps may rejoice together.

R.35: But I tell you, look up and see the fields! The grain is ripe and ready to harvest.
R.36: Already the harvester is getting paid and is gathering a crop for eternal life. So the one who plants and the one who harvests can be glad together.

decisions.choice: white: grain ripened and turned pale, ready to cut
decisions.reason: Ripe wheat and barley turn from green to pale gold. Jesus speaks of the fields, and at the same time of the Samaritans who are coming out of the town toward him (4:30): they are the harvest that is ready now.

decisions.choice: already begins the next sentence: already the reaper is being paid
alternatives: already ends the sentence before: white for harvest already
decisions.reason: The manuscripts have no punctuation, and the word can end the sentence before or begin this one. The SBLGNT punctuates it with what follows, and John often puts "already" at the head of a clause (4:51; 7:14). The other reading, "white already for harvest", is old and well known from the King James Version, so a footnote gives it. Verse 36 is printed from "Already", as the punctuation suggests, though in the verse division the word stands at the end of verse 35.

decisions.choice: the harvest of the last days: people gathered for eternal life
decisions.reason: The prophets spoke of God's final gathering as a harvest (Isaiah 27:12; Joel 3:13), and Jesus uses the image for people gathered to God (Matthew 9:37-38). Here the wage is the joy of the work, and the crop is people brought to eternal life.

decisions.choice: sower and reaper rejoice together: harvest comes straight after sowing
alternatives: no echo; only the shared joy is meant
decisions.reason: Normally sowing and reaping are months apart (verse 35), and the sower may never see the crop. Here they rejoice at the same time. Amos 9:13 pictures the age to come in the same way: the one plowing will overtake the one reaping. The link to Amos is possible but not stated.

decisions.choice: eternal life
alternatives: the life of the age to come
decisions.reason: The book-wide key term for John, kept at every level.

decisions.choice: white
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the picture of pale ripe grain; Readable says "ripe" so that young readers do not imagine snow (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: Listen (B); But (R)
decisions.reason: The word calls attention to what follows; the style guide keeps "behold" out of modern English.

decisions.choice: is being paid / is getting paid
decisions.reason: Plain words for a worker's pay.

records.source: ἐν γὰρ τούτῳ ὁ λόγος ἐστὶν ἀληθινὸς ὅτι Ἄλλος ἐστὶν ὁ σπείρων καὶ ἄλλος ὁ θερίζων·
records.gloss: For in this the saying is true that, "Another is the one sowing and another the one reaping."

L.37: For in this the saying is true: 'One is the one who sows, and another the one who reaps.'

R.37: People say, 'One person plants and someone else harvests.' And here that saying is true.

decisions.choice: the saying is true: the proverb really fits this case
alternatives: the saying is merely accurate in general
decisions.reason: The adjective means true in the sense of genuine, holding good. "In this" points to the situation Jesus has just described.

decisions.choice: a saying that usually complained of unfairness
decisions.reason: The Old Testament uses the thought as a curse or a lament: one sows and another eats the crop (Deuteronomy 28:30; Job 31:8; Micah 6:15). Here the same fact becomes a reason for shared joy (verse 36): others did the sowing, and the disciples reap.

decisions.choice: the saying first, then that it is true
alternatives: For in this the saying is true: ...
decisions.reason: Readable gives the saying before saying that it fits, which is easier to follow.

decisions.choice: one person ... another / someone else
decisions.reason: The words refer to anyone who sows or reaps; plain words for a person need no gender setting.

records.source: ἐγὼ ἀπέστειλα ὑμᾶς θερίζειν ὃ οὐχ ὑμεῖς κεκοπιάκατε· ἄλλοι κεκοπιάκασιν, καὶ ὑμεῖς εἰς τὸν κόπον αὐτῶν εἰσεληλύθατε.
records.gloss: I sent you to reap what not you have toiled; others have toiled, and you into the toil of them have entered.

L.38: I sent you to reap what you have not toiled over; others have toiled, and you have entered into their toil."

R.38: I sent you to harvest a crop that you did not work for. Other people did the hard work before you, and now you are gathering what they worked for."

decisions.choice: I sent you: spoken as already done
decisions.reason: The disciples have not yet been sent out in this Gospel (17:18; 20:21). The past tense may look back to their call to follow him, or speak of their mission as already settled. The Samaritans coming out to Jesus (4:30) are the first crop they share in; later the apostles would preach in Samaria (Acts 8:4-25). The evidence does not settle which is meant.

decisions.choice: others: those who worked before the disciples, not named
alternatives: John the Baptist and the prophets before him
the woman who brought her townspeople
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say who the others are. Jesus himself has just done the work in Samaria, and the woman has brought the town to him; the prophets and John the Baptist had prepared the ground before. Every level keeps "others" without naming them.

decisions.choice: toil: hard, wearying labor
decisions.reason: The verb and noun speak of tiring work. The same verb describes Jesus at the well, "tired from the journey" (4:6): the toil others have done includes his own.

decisions.choice: toiled, toil (L); labor (B)
decisions.reason: Literal repeats one word three times as the Greek does; Balanced keeps the sense of hard labor.

decisions.choice: Other people ... before you
decisions.reason: Readable shows that their work came first; the masculine plural refers to anyone, so plain "people" needs no setting.

records.source: Ἐκ δὲ τῆς πόλεως ἐκείνης πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτὸν τῶν Σαμαριτῶν διὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς γυναικὸς μαρτυρούσης ὅτι Εἶπέν μοι πάντα ἃ ἐποίησα.
records.gloss: From now the city that many believed in him of the Samaritans because of the word of the woman testifying that, "He told me all things which I did."

L.39: And from that town many of the Samaritans believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} because of the word of the woman who testified, "He told me all the things that I did."

R.39: Many Samaritans from that town believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} because of what the woman said. She told them, "He told me all the things I have ever done."

decisions.choice: believed in him: put their trust in Jesus
decisions.reason: "Believe in" with a person is John's phrase for trusting the person (2:11). They came to trust Jesus because of what she said, the way the Gospel expects later readers to believe through others' testimony (17:20; 20:31).

decisions.choice: testified: she bore witness
decisions.reason: John uses this verb for John the Baptist's witness to Jesus (1:7, 15, 32-34). The woman becomes a witness in the same way.

decisions.choice: the woman's word, set against Jesus's own word (4:41)
decisions.reason: John contrasts the word of the woman with the word of Jesus himself, which leads many more to believe (4:41-42). Her testimony brings them to him; his word makes their belief their own.

decisions.choice: Samaritans, with no gender setting
decisions.reason: The Samaritans who believed were men and women, and the word "Samaritans" already includes both, so no setting is needed.

decisions.choice: word
decisions.reason: Keeps the repeated word that sets her word against his (meaning decision m3); Readable says "what the woman said" and "what Jesus said" to keep the same contrast.

records.heading: Many Samaritans believe

records.source: ὡς οὖν ἦλθον πρὸς αὐτὸν οἱ Σαμαρῖται, ἠρώτων αὐτὸν μεῖναι παρ’ αὐτοῖς· καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐκεῖ δύο ἡμέρας.
records.gloss: When therefore came to him the Samaritans, they were asking him to stay with them; and he stayed there two days.

L.40: So when the Samaritans came to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they were asking {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to stay with them; and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stayed there two days.

R.40: The Samaritans came to Jesus and asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} again and again to stay with them. So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} stayed there for two days.

decisions.choice: a Jew staying as a guest of Samaritans
decisions.reason: Jews and Samaritans did not usually share things (4:9). Here Samaritans invite a Jewish teacher into their homes, and he accepts, eating and lodging with them.

decisions.choice: stay: lodge with them, with the deeper sense of remaining
decisions.reason: The verb is the ordinary one for staying as a guest, as at 1:38-39, and here it is meant plainly. It is the same verb Jesus later uses for remaining in him (15:4-10).

decisions.choice: stay, stayed
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: the natural word in its ordinary sense.

decisions.choice: kept asking (B); asked again and again (R)
decisions.reason: Shows the repeated request of the imperfect verb.

records.source: καὶ πολλῷ πλείους ἐπίστευσαν διὰ τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ, τῇ τε γυναικὶ ἔλεγον ὅτι Οὐκέτι διὰ τὴν σὴν λαλιὰν πιστεύομεν· αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἀκηκόαμεν, καὶ οἴδαμεν ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου.
records.gloss: And by much more believed because of the word of him, \v 42 and to the woman they were saying that, "No longer because of your speech do we believe; for ourselves we have heard, and we know that this one is truly the Savior of the world."

L.41: And many more believed because of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word,
L.42: and they were saying to the woman, "No longer because of your talk do we believe, for we ourselves have heard, and we know that this [one] is truly the Savior of the world."

R.41: Many more people believed because of what Jesus said.
R.42: They told the woman, "At first we believed because of what you told us. But now we believe because we have heard {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for ourselves. We know that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} really is the Savior of the world, the one who saves people everywhere."

decisions.choice: many more: a much larger number
decisions.reason: The phrase is "more by much", a comparison of number: many more Samaritans came to believe than the first group.

decisions.choice: your talk: what she had told them
decisions.reason: λαλιὰν means speech or what someone says, and it can mean mere talk. Set beside the "word" of Jesus it is the lesser thing, but they are not scorning her: her report brought them to him (4:39). Now they believe on firsthand hearing.

decisions.choice: they have heard for themselves and know
decisions.reason: Their belief no longer rests on another's report but on Jesus's own word. Both verbs are perfects: what they have heard and know stays with them.

decisions.choice: the Savior: a title for God himself, here given to Jesus
alternatives: a deliverer in a general sense
