decisions.reason: In the Old Testament God is Israel's Savior (Isaiah 43:3, 11; 45:15, 21). In the Roman world rulers, the emperors among them, were also hailed as saviors. Only here in John's Gospel is Jesus called Savior; 1 John 4:14 says, "the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world".

decisions.choice: the world: humanity as a whole, Samaritans as well as Jews
decisions.reason: Key term. Here κόσμου means all people. Jesus told the woman that salvation is from the Jews (4:22); Samaritans now confess that it is for the whole world (compare 1:29; 3:16-17).

decisions.choice: the Savior of the world (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the Christ, the Savior of the world (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "the Christ" before "the Savior", as the King James Version reflects. The older manuscripts do not have it. A footnote gives it; a reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: At first we believed because of what you told us. But now
alternatives: We no longer believe because of your words
decisions.reason: "No longer" implies that they had first believed on her word; Readable says so in two plain sentences.

decisions.choice: the one who saves people everywhere
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the title and adds what it means here (meaning decisions m4 and m5).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: "This one" is Jesus; Balanced and Readable use the pronoun with the deity_pronoun setting.

records.source: Μετὰ δὲ τὰς δύο ἡμέρας ἐξῆλθεν ἐκεῖθεν εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν·
records.gloss: After now the two days he went out from there into the Galilee;

L.43: And after the two days {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went out from there into Galilee.

R.43: After those two days, Jesus left that place and went on to Galilee.

decisions.choice: the journey of 4:3 resumes
decisions.reason: Jesus had left Judea for Galilee and passed through Samaria on the way (4:3-4). After two days with the Samaritans he goes on.

decisions.choice: he went out from there (SBLGNT)
alternatives: he went out from there and went away (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "and went away". The sense is the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus at the start of a new scene.

records.heading: Jesus heals an official's son

records.source: αὐτὸς γὰρ Ἰησοῦς ἐμαρτύρησεν ὅτι προφήτης ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ πατρίδι τιμὴν οὐκ ἔχει.
records.gloss: Himself for Jesus testified that a prophet in the own homeland honor not has.

L.44: For Jesus {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} testified that a prophet in his own homeland has no honor.

R.44: Jesus {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} had said that people do not honor a prophet in his own home country.

decisions.choice: his own homeland: left open, as the text leaves it
alternatives: Galilee, his home region (Nazareth): he goes there knowing he will not be truly honored
Judea and Jerusalem: he leaves because he was not honored there
decisions.reason: Matthew 13:57, Mark 6:4 and Luke 4:24 use the saying of Nazareth in Galilee, and John calls Jesus a Galilean (1:46; 7:41, 52). But verse 45 says the Galileans welcomed him, which is hard to fit with a saying meant to explain why he went there. On one view his homeland is Galilee, and their welcome is not real honor, since it rests on the signs they saw (2:23-25; 4:48). On another it is Judea, with Jerusalem, the city of David from whose line the Messiah came (7:42); he "came to his own, and his own did not receive him" (1:11), so he left it. The evidence is balanced, and every level keeps "his own homeland" without naming it.

decisions.choice: Jesus himself had said it: a comment by the narrator
decisions.reason: "For" introduces John's explanation of the journey. "Himself" stresses that the saying was Jesus's own. The past tense looks back to something Jesus had said, not to a word spoken at this point.

decisions.choice: homeland: the land or town of one's family
decisions.reason: The word can mean a home town or a native country, which is why the question in m1 arises.

decisions.choice: had declared (B); had said (R)
decisions.reason: Shows that John is recalling a saying (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: his own homeland, with no gender setting
decisions.reason: The proverb pictures a prophet like those of Israel, and here it is applied to Jesus; it is kept as it stands.

records.source: ὅτε οὖν ἦλθεν εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν, ἐδέξαντο αὐτὸν οἱ Γαλιλαῖοι, πάντα ἑωρακότες ὅσα ἐποίησεν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ, καὶ αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἦλθον εἰς τὴν ἑορτήν.
records.gloss: When therefore he came into the Galilee, received him the Galileans, all things having seen as many as he did in Jerusalem at the feast, also themselves for came to the feast.

L.45: So when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came into Galilee, the Galileans received {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, having seen all the things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did in Jerusalem at the feast; for they themselves also had gone to the feast.

R.45: When Jesus arrived in Galilee, the people there welcomed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They had gone to the Passover festival in Jerusalem too, and they had seen all the things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did there.

decisions.choice: the feast: the Passover of 2:13-23
decisions.reason: Galilean pilgrims went up to Jerusalem for the festivals (Luke 2:41-44). At that Passover Jesus cleared the temple courts and did signs that led many to believe (2:23).

decisions.choice: a welcome based on what they had seen
alternatives: a welcome that shows full faith
decisions.reason: Their welcome rests on the signs they saw. John has already said that Jesus did not entrust himself to belief of that kind (2:23-25), and his words in verse 48 point the same way. This bears on the saying in verse 44.

decisions.choice: the Passover festival
decisions.reason: Readable names the feast meant (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: the journey first, then what they saw
alternatives: having seen ..., for they too had gone
decisions.reason: Readable puts the events in the order they happened.

records.source: Ἦλθεν οὖν πάλιν εἰς τὴν Κανὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, ὅπου ἐποίησεν τὸ ὕδωρ οἶνον.
records.gloss: He came therefore again to the Cana of the Galilee, where he made the water wine.

L.46: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came again to Cana of Galilee, where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had made the water [into] wine.

R.46: Jesus went back to Cana in Galilee. This was the town where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had changed water into wine.

decisions.choice: a reminder of the first sign at Cana (2:1-11)
decisions.reason: John points back to the first sign so that readers connect the two. The second sign also happens from Cana (4:54), and the two stories have much in common: a request, an answer that seems to hold back, trust in Jesus's word, and belief as the result (2:5, 11; 4:50, 53).

decisions.choice: had changed ... into
decisions.reason: Natural wording for the event of 2:9.

records.source: καὶ ἦν τις βασιλικὸς οὗ ὁ υἱὸς ἠσθένει ἐν Καφαρναούμ.
records.gloss: And there was a certain royal official whose the son was sick in Capernaum.

L.46: And there was a certain royal official whose son was sick in Capernaum.

R.46: In the town of Capernaum there was an official of the king who ruled Galilee. His son was sick.

decisions.choice: a royal official: most likely an officer of Herod Antipas
alternatives: a member of the royal family
decisions.reason: βασιλικὸς means someone belonging to the king, in his service. In Galilee the ruler was Herod Antipas (4 BC to AD 39); his title was tetrarch, but people called him king (Mark 6:14). The official could have been Jewish or Gentile; John does not say. Matthew 8:5-13 and Luke 7:1-10 tell of a centurion at Capernaum whose servant Jesus healed from a distance; John's account differs in its details, and whether it is the same event is not settled.

decisions.choice: Capernaum: a town on the Sea of Galilee, a long walk from Cana
decisions.reason: Capernaum lay on the north shore of the lake, far below Cana in the hills (compare 2:12), about 15 to 20 miles away; the exact site of Cana is not certain. Jesus's word reaches the boy without his going there.

decisions.choice: an official of the king who ruled Galilee
decisions.reason: Readable says what "royal" means here (meaning decision m1) without naming Herod, which the text does not do.

decisions.choice: the place first, then the son's illness
decisions.reason: Readable sets the scene in two short sentences.

records.source: οὗτος ἀκούσας ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἥκει ἐκ τῆς Ἰουδαίας εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν ἀπῆλθεν πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ ἠρώτα ἵνα καταβῇ καὶ ἰάσηται αὐτοῦ τὸν υἱόν, ἤμελλεν γὰρ ἀποθνῄσκειν.
records.gloss: This one, having heard that Jesus has come out of the Judea into the Galilee, went away to him and was asking that he would come down and heal his the son, he was about for to die.

L.47: This [man], having heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, went away to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and was asking that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would come down and heal his son, for he was about to die.

R.47: He heard that Jesus had come back from Judea to Galilee. So he went to Jesus and begged {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to come down to Capernaum and make his son well. His son was about to die.

decisions.choice: was asking: kept pleading
decisions.reason: The imperfect shows a request made again and again. The same verb was used of the Samaritans' request in 4:40.

decisions.choice: come down: from the hill country of Cana to the lakeshore
decisions.reason: Capernaum is far lower than Cana, so one goes "down" to it (2:12). The official asks Jesus to come with him; he assumes the healing needs Jesus to be there.

decisions.choice: he was about to die: at the point of death
alternatives: he was going to die someday
decisions.reason: The verb means to be on the verge of something. The boy was dying.

decisions.choice: to Capernaum
decisions.reason: Readable names the place (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: the boy
decisions.reason: Shows that the son, not the father, was dying.

records.source: εἶπεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς πρὸς αὐτόν· Ἐὰν μὴ σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα ἴδητε, οὐ μὴ πιστεύσητε.
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jesus to him, "Unless signs and wonders you see, not not you will believe."

L.48: So Jesus said to him, "Unless you [people] see signs and wonders, you will certainly not believe."

R.48: Jesus said to the man, "You people will not believe unless you see signs and wonders."

decisions.choice: you: plural, spoken to the man but about the people at large
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks to the official, but both verbs are plural. His words take in the Galileans who welcomed him because of what they had seen (4:45), and the official with them.

decisions.choice: signs and wonders: the phrase for the deeds of the exodus
decisions.reason: The pair is used in the Old Testament for what God did in Egypt (Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 4:34; 6:22). It appears only here in John. Joined with "wonders", "signs" here means the striking deed itself rather than what it points to.

decisions.choice: a warning against belief that waits for proof
decisions.reason: The double negative (οὐ μὴ) makes the statement strong: without such deeds you will not believe at all. Jesus does not refuse the man; he challenges a belief that depends on seeing (2:23-25; 20:29). The man answers by pleading again, and then believes Jesus's word before he sees anything (4:50).

decisions.choice: [people] (L); None of you (B); You people (R)
decisions.reason: Shows that "you" is plural (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: certainly not
decisions.reason: Literal shows the strong double negative (meaning decision m3).

records.source: λέγει πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁ βασιλικός· Κύριε, κατάβηθι πρὶν ἀποθανεῖν τὸ παιδίον μου.
records.gloss: Says to him the royal official, "Sir, come down before dies the little child of me."

L.49: The royal official says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Sir, come down before my little child dies."

R.49: The official said, "Sir, please come before my child dies!"

decisions.choice: Sir: a respectful address
alternatives: Lord, a confession of who Jesus is
decisions.reason: The address is the polite form used to anyone of standing; the Samaritan woman uses it at 4:11, 15 and 19. The official does not yet know who Jesus is; he believes later (4:53). A footnote gives "Lord".

decisions.choice: my little child: a tender word
decisions.reason: The father uses a diminutive, "little child". John calls the boy his son, and the servants call him "the boy" (4:51).

decisions.choice: he does not give up
decisions.reason: Like Jesus's mother at Cana (2:3-5), the official is not turned away by Jesus's reply; he simply asks again.

decisions.choice: Sir
decisions.reason: Shows the polite address (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: please
decisions.reason: Readable shows the urgent pleading in the words.

decisions.choice: pleaded
decisions.reason: His words are an urgent plea, which the verb shows.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Πορεύου· ὁ υἱός σου ζῇ.
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "Go; the son of you lives."

L.50: Jesus says to him, "Go; your son lives."

R.50: Jesus told him, "Go home. Your son is alive and well."

decisions.choice: lives: will not die, is well again
alternatives: will live (a promise about the future)
decisions.reason: The verb is present: the boy lives now. In Hebrew usage, to "live" after an illness is to recover (2 Kings 1:2; 8:8-10). Verse 53 shows that the healing happened at the moment Jesus spoke.

decisions.choice: possibly an echo of Elijah: "See, your son lives" (1 Kings 17:23)
alternatives: no echo; the words are ordinary
decisions.reason: Elijah gave a widow back her son with almost the same words in the Greek Old Testament. The phrase is ordinary enough to occur without any echo, so the link is uncertain.

decisions.choice: Go: Jesus sends him home without coming
decisions.reason: The official asked Jesus to come down. Jesus does not go; he speaks the word and sends the father on his way.

decisions.choice: is alive and well
decisions.reason: Readable says what "lives" means here (meaning decision m1). Literal and Balanced keep "lives", which carries the echo (m2) and returns in verses 51 and 53.

decisions.choice: home
decisions.reason: Readable says where he is to go.

records.source: ἐπίστευσεν ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῷ λόγῳ ὃν εἶπεν αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ ἐπορεύετο.
records.gloss: Believed the man the word that said to him the Jesus and was going.

L.50: The man believed the word which Jesus said to him, and set out.

R.50: The man believed what Jesus told him, and he started back home.

decisions.choice: he believed Jesus's word before seeing anything
decisions.reason: "Believe" with the word as its object means accepting that what Jesus said is true. Jesus had said that people believe only when they see (4:48); this man believes the word alone. When the word proves true, he believes in the fuller sense (4:53).

decisions.choice: was going: was on his way
decisions.reason: The imperfect leaves him on the road, where the servants meet him (4:51).

decisions.choice: started for home / started back home
decisions.reason: Says where he went; Literal "set out" keeps the bare verb.

records.source: ἤδη δὲ αὐτοῦ καταβαίνοντος οἱ δοῦλοι αὐτοῦ ὑπήντησαν αὐτῷ λέγοντες ὅτι ὁ παῖς αὐτοῦ ζῇ.
records.gloss: Already now he going down, the slaves of him met him, saying that the boy of him lives.

L.51: And while he was already going down, his slaves met him, saying that his boy lives.

R.51: While he was still on his way home, his servants came to meet him. They told him, "Your son is alive and well!"

decisions.choice: household slaves, owned by the official
decisions.reason: δοῦλοι were slaves belonging to the household, not hired staff. A royal official would have had several. They come out to give the news.

decisions.choice: his boy: the official's son
decisions.reason: The word can mean a boy or a servant; here it is the son of verse 46, as "his son" in verse 53 shows.

decisions.choice: lives: the word Jesus used
decisions.reason: The servants' news repeats Jesus's word "lives" (4:50), and verse 53 repeats it again. John uses the repetition to show that the word came true.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m1) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

decisions.choice: direct speech: "Your son is alive and well!"
decisions.reason: Readable gives their words as they spoke them, which is easier to follow, and uses the same words as verse 50.

records.source: ἐπύθετο οὖν τὴν ὥραν παρ’ αὐτῶν ἐν ᾗ κομψότερον ἔσχεν· εἶπαν οὖν αὐτῷ ὅτι Ἐχθὲς ὥραν ἑβδόμην ἀφῆκεν αὐτὸν ὁ πυρετός.
records.gloss: He inquired therefore the hour from them in which better he had; they said therefore to him that, "Yesterday [at the] hour seventh left him the fever."
pieces: at about one in the afternoon

L.52: So he asked them the hour in which he had gotten better; so they said to him, "Yesterday at [the] seventh hour the fever left him."

R.52: He asked them when his son had started to get better. They said, "Yesterday, at about one o'clock in the afternoon, the fever went away."

decisions.choice: he had begun to get better
decisions.reason: The phrase means to be better, to be on the mend. The father asks when the improvement began; the servants answer that the fever left him altogether.

decisions.choice: the seventh hour: about one in the afternoon
alternatives: about seven in the morning, counting from midnight
decisions.reason: Hours were counted from sunrise, about six in the morning, so the seventh hour was about one in the afternoon (see 1:39; 11:9). Some have argued that John counts from midnight, which would make it seven in the morning. A footnote gives the literal wording and the other way of counting.

decisions.choice: yesterday: the father reached home the next day
decisions.reason: The journey down to Capernaum was long, so the father met his servants the following day. A Jewish day began at sunset, so if they met after nightfall, the afternoon before was already "yesterday" even if he had traveled only a few hours.

decisions.choice: about one in the afternoon
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: Literal keeps the clock time, and Balanced and Readable give the modern time (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: the boy (B); his son (R)
decisions.reason: Shows who got better.

records.source: ἔγνω οὖν ὁ πατὴρ ὅτι ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ ἐν ᾗ εἶπεν αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ὁ υἱός σου ζῇ, καὶ ἐπίστευσεν αὐτὸς καὶ ἡ οἰκία αὐτοῦ ὅλη.
records.gloss: Knew therefore the father that [it was] in that the hour in which said to him the Jesus, "The son of you lives," and believed he himself and the household of him whole.

L.53: So the father knew that [it was] at that hour in which Jesus said to him, "Your son lives," and he himself believed, and his whole household.

R.53: Then the father realized that this was the exact time when Jesus had said to him, "Your son is alive and well." So he and everyone in his home believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: he believed: he became a believer in Jesus
alternatives: he believed the word again, as in verse 50
decisions.reason: In verse 50 he believed what Jesus said. Here the verb stands without an object, as in 1:50 and 20:29: he now believes in Jesus himself. The story moves from asking for a sign, to trusting the word, to belief.

decisions.choice: his whole household: family and servants
decisions.reason: A household included the family and its slaves and dependents. In Acts whole households come to believe together (Acts 10:2, 44; 16:15, 31-34; 18:8).

decisions.choice: the father: the official is now named by his relation to the boy
decisions.reason: John calls him a royal official (4:46, 49), then the man (4:50), and now the father. The title gives way to the parent whose son lives.

decisions.choice: in him
decisions.reason: Readable says whom they believed in (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: is alive and well
decisions.reason: As in verse 50.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ πάλιν δεύτερον σημεῖον ἐποίησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐλθὼν ἐκ τῆς Ἰουδαίας εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν.
records.gloss: This now again second sign did the Jesus having come out of the Judea into the Galilee.

L.54: And this again [was the] second sign [that] Jesus did, having come from Judea into Galilee.

R.54: This was the second sign Jesus did. It happened after {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came back to Galilee from Judea.

decisions.choice: again a second sign: the second sign, counted from 2:11
alternatives: a second sign done on a second journey from Judea
decisions.reason: "Again" and "second" together stress the count. The first sign was at Cana (2:11); John mentions other signs in Jerusalem (2:23) but does not number them. The count marks the two signs at Cana, which frame the story from 2:1 to 4:54.

decisions.choice: sign: a deed that points to who Jesus is
decisions.reason: Key term in John (2:11). Here the sign shows that Jesus's word gives life, from a distance and at once (compare 5:24-25).

decisions.choice: "again" not repeated
alternatives: this again was the second sign
decisions.reason: "Again" with "second" says the same thing twice (meaning decision m1); Literal keeps it.
